item.title: Making Tax Digital Income Thresholds: Which Landlords Need to Comply?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Revenue & Customs' Making Tax Digital (MTD) initiative is transforming how landlords report their income, with phased rollouts affecting property investors at different thresholds. The scheme requires digital record-keeping and quarterly submissions through compatible software, but not all landlords need to comply immediately.

Current MTD Requirements for Property Investors

Since April 2023, landlords with combined property and self-employment income exceeding £50,000 annually must follow MTD rules. This threshold is calculated before expenses, meaning gross rental income from all properties determines eligibility. Those meeting this requirement should already be submitting quarterly updates through approved software alongside their annual tax return.

For landlords whose total qualifying income sits between £30,000 and £50,000, the compliance date is set for April 2025. This gives mid-range property investors additional time to prepare their systems and familiarise themselves with the digital submission process.

Exemptions and Special Cases

Landlords with property income below £30,000 annually remain outside MTD for now, though HMRC may review these thresholds in future. Some property owners might be surprised to learn that income from multiple properties combines towards the total - owning several modestly yielding properties could push investors over the threshold even if individual rentals generate modest returns.

Jointly owned properties require particular attention, as each owner must declare their share of the income. For example, spouses splitting rental income 50-50 would each need to assess whether their portion meets the relevant threshold. Trustees and non-resident landlords also face special considerations under the MTD framework.

Preparing for Digital Tax Reporting

Landlords approaching the thresholds may wish to consider several preparatory steps. Transitioning to digital accounting software well in advance can smooth the compliance process, allowing time to resolve any technical issues. Many providers now offer MTD-compatible solutions tailored to property businesses, some integrating directly with banking platforms.

Those affected might also review their record-keeping practices, as MTD requires maintaining digital records throughout the tax year rather than compiling information annually. Professional advice could prove valuable, particularly for landlords with complex portfolios or those who need clarification on how specific expenses should be recorded under the new system.

As HMRC continues expanding its digital tax initiative, staying informed about upcoming changes remains crucial for all property investors. While the current thresholds provide some landlords with additional time, the direction of travel suggests digital reporting will eventually become universal for tax purposes.

item.title: Agents face new rules from today
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New regulations governing damp and mould investigations in rental properties have come into effect in Scotland. The Investigation and Commencement of Repair (Scotland) Regulations 2026 sets out clear deadlines for landlords and letting agents to address these issues, marking a significant shift in property management practices. These changes aim to ensure tenants receive timely responses to concerns about damp and mould, which can have serious implications for health and property maintenance.

Key deadlines for landlords and agents

Under the new rules, landlords are required to act swiftly when damp or mould concerns are raised. Once informed of a potential issue, they must carry out an investigation within 10 working days. Following the investigation, tenants must receive a written summary of the findings within three working days. If repairs are deemed necessary, work must commence within five working days of the investigation’s conclusion. These strict timelines mean landlords and letting agents may need to review their current processes to ensure compliance.

Practical considerations include arranging timely property inspections, maintaining accurate records, and ensuring access to reliable contractors. In cases where the source of damp or mould is unclear, landlords may need to seek specialist expertise. This could present challenges, particularly in rural areas where contractors and damp specialists may be less readily available.

Operational implications for letting agents

The new regulations place additional responsibilities on letting agents, who must ensure their internal processes align with the updated requirements. This includes establishing robust systems for identifying and addressing damp and mould issues promptly. Clear communication with tenants, thorough record-keeping, and access to competent contractors will be essential to meeting the deadlines.

Propertymark, a leading professional body for the property sector, has highlighted the importance of these changes. Hazel MacIver, Policy and Campaigns Officer at Propertymark, stated: “The new duties on damp and mould represent an important change for letting agents and landlords in Scotland. The timescales are clear, and agents will need to have robust processes in place from the point they become aware of a potential issue.”

Landlords unable to meet the deadlines due to circumstances beyond their control, such as contractor unavailability, must inform tenants promptly and explain the delay. They are also expected to take reasonable steps to minimise the impact on tenants where possible.

These regulations aim to improve living conditions for tenants while ensuring landlords and agents handle damp and mould issues efficiently. For those managing rental properties in Scotland, adapting to these changes will be crucial in maintaining compliance and safeguarding tenant wellbeing.

item.title: Investors pile £4.2bn into one of property’s fastest-growing sectors
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK Build to Rent (BTR) sector has seen £4.2bn in investment during 2026, with single-family homes driving much of this activity. New data from Knight Frank reveals £1.6bn was committed in the third quarter alone, with two-thirds of deals focusing on this fast-growing segment.

Single-family homes dominate BTR investment

Single-family housing accounted for 67% of all Build to Rent investment in Q3 2026, with over £1bn deployed across 11 significant transactions. This reflects growing investor confidence in properties designed for family living, which now represent one of property's most dynamic sectors.

Operational BTR assets also proved attractive, drawing £600m during the quarter - 38% of total investment. Two major portfolio deals contributed £500m of this figure. Established assets offering immediate rental income have accounted for 61% of all BTR investment this year, as investors prioritise platforms capable of delivering scale and reliable returns.

Investor confidence returns despite economic headwinds

Knight Frank analysts describe Q3 as a potential turning point for the market, with several high-profile transactions demonstrating renewed investor appetite. The £400m acquisition by Border to Coast Pension Partnership from Blackstone ranked among the quarter's largest deals.

Lizzie Breckner, Knight Frank's Head of Build to Rent Research, noted: "While the market remains selective given macroeconomic conditions, capital continues to target opportunities with strong fundamentals. The growing proportion of operational transactions reflects investor focus on assets that can deliver immediate income alongside future rental growth."

Nick Pleydell-Bouverie, Head of Residential Investment at Knight Frank, observed: "Single-family housing continues to attract significant capital from both domestic and international investors, alongside growing pension fund interest. The sector's strong occupier demand and proven track record make it particularly appealing."

What this means for the UK rental market

The surge in Build to Rent investment, particularly in family-oriented properties, suggests institutional investors are responding to fundamental shifts in housing demand. As traditional buy-to-let landlords face increasing challenges, professionally-managed rental homes appear poised to play a bigger role in addressing the UK's housing needs.

With operational assets attracting the majority of investment, the data indicates a maturing market where investors increasingly value proven platforms over development opportunities. This trend towards stabilised income streams may influence the types of rental properties coming to market in coming years.

item.title: Rental stock down by up to 42% in Q3
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK rental market has seen a notable contraction in available properties during the third quarter of the year, with some regions experiencing declines of up to 42%. This sharp reduction in rental stock comes amidst a series of recent regulatory changes that have reshaped the landscape for both landlords and tenants.

Regional Variations in Rental Availability

Analysis of the rental market across England reveals significant regional disparities in property availability. While some areas have maintained relatively stable levels of rental stock, others have witnessed dramatic decreases. This geographical variation highlights the complex nature of the housing market and the differing impacts of recent reforms across the country.

Impact of Regulatory Changes

The substantial reduction in rental properties coincides with the introduction of new housing regulations and tax reforms. These changes, designed to improve tenant protections and address housing affordability, appear to have influenced landlord behaviour. Some property owners may be reconsidering their positions in the rental market, potentially leading to decreased supply.

Key factors contributing to this trend include:

  • Increased regulatory requirements for landlords
  • Changes to mortgage interest tax relief
  • Enhanced tenant rights legislation
  • Rising costs associated with property maintenance

Implications for the Rental Market

The contraction in rental stock could have several consequences for the UK housing market. With fewer properties available, tenants may face increased competition for suitable accommodation, potentially driving up rental prices in certain areas. This situation may also encourage some prospective tenants to explore alternative housing options, such as shared accommodation or longer-term leases.

For landlords and property investors, the changing market conditions may prompt a reassessment of investment strategies. Some might consider diversifying their portfolios or exploring different property types, while others could choose to exit the rental market altogether.

The third quarter's rental market trends underscore the evolving nature of the UK property sector. As the market continues to adapt to new regulations and economic pressures, both landlords and tenants may need to adjust their expectations and strategies in this changing landscape.

item.title: Rightmove backs new podcast featuring 10 estate agency leaders
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property portal Rightmove has partnered with industry expert Silvia Eldawi to launch a new podcast series showcasing insights from leading UK estate and letting agents. Golden Nuggets: Movers & Shakers debuts today, offering 40 episodes over October and November with each instalment running for around 15 minutes.

Industry expertise in bite-sized episodes

The podcast will feature ten agency leaders from regions including London, Wales, Yorkshire and the South West discussing key industry topics. Listeners can expect practical discussions around sales strategies, technological advancements, artificial intelligence applications and enhancing customer experiences.

Eldawi, who brings over 20 years of property experience to the hosting role, emphasises the value of real-world insights: "Having spent decades in this sector, I've found the most valuable lessons come from those who've navigated the challenges firsthand. This series creates a space for honest reflections about what works in today's market."

Supporting professional development

Rightmove will supplement the podcast with consumer-facing content including video highlights and moving guides featuring advice from participating agents. Christian Balshen, Rightmove's director of agent partnerships, notes: "This initiative helps busy professionals learn from peers in an accessible format. Podcasts deliver concentrated knowledge without demanding large time commitments."

The series forms part of Rightmove's broader support for industry professionals, complementing existing webinar programmes and development events. With new episodes released each weekday, the production schedule allows agents to stay informed alongside their daily responsibilities.

Featured contributors include directors from Proceed Property (South Wales & Bristol), Moovahome (Swindon), Fine & Country (West London) and several other established agencies across England and Wales. Their collective experience promises diverse perspectives on navigating the current property landscape.

Golden Nuggets: Movers & Shakers is available via major platforms including YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts, making professional insights accessible whether agents are commuting, between viewings or preparing market appraisals.

item.title: Tories pledge to scrap stamp duty and slash £50,000 from new-build costs
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Conservative Party has recently announced ambitious plans to reform the UK housing market, including proposals to scrap stamp duty and reduce the cost of new-build homes by up to £50,000. Unveiled at the party’s conference in Birmingham, the plans aim to streamline regulations and boost housing supply, though some industry experts have raised questions about their feasibility and potential impact.

Key Proposals for Housing Reform

The Conservatives have labelled their proposals as the “biggest deregulation project in a generation.” Among the key measures is the abolition of stamp duty on property purchases, a move designed to make homeownership more accessible. Additionally, the party plans to overhaul housebuilding regulations by scrapping the Future Homes Standard and proposed low-carbon heating requirements, which they argue add unnecessary costs to construction.

Another significant change involves replacing Section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy with a single developer charge. The party claims this would simplify the planning process and accelerate housing development. Furthermore, the Conservatives propose abolishing Natural England and the Environment Agency, transferring their functions to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.

Industry Reactions and Concerns

While the proposals have been welcomed by some industry figures for their focus on increasing housing supply, others have expressed caution. Timothy Douglas, head of policy and campaigns at Propertymark, praised the emphasis on simplifying planning and reducing barriers to development. However, he questioned whether the claimed £50,000 reduction in new-build costs would ultimately benefit buyers.

Douglas also highlighted the importance of balancing cost savings with quality and standards, particularly regarding the potential scrapping of the Future Homes Standard. He noted that while planning reform is crucial, it alone cannot solve the UK’s ongoing housing crisis. “Policy makers must not make cost saving at the expense of quality and standards,” he added.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith emphasised the party’s commitment to tax cuts, stating that it would aim to abolish at least one tax in every Budget under a future Conservative government. Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam echoed this sentiment, calling for fewer regulations to facilitate housing and infrastructure development.

What Could This Mean for Homeowners?

For prospective buyers and homeowners, these proposals could signal significant changes to the housing market. The abolition of stamp duty might make purchasing a property more affordable, particularly for first-time buyers. Meanwhile, the proposed simplification of planning regulations could lead to an increase in housing supply, potentially easing the current shortage.

However, the long-term impact of these reforms remains uncertain. Homeowners may wish to monitor developments closely, particularly regarding how changes to environmental standards and planning processes could affect the quality and sustainability of new homes.

As the Conservative Party’s proposals continue to generate debate, it is clear that any reforms will need to strike a careful balance between reducing costs, increasing supply, and maintaining high standards in the UK housing market.

item.title: Mortgage shock as 99% of cheaper fixed deals vanish
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK mortgage market has seen significant shifts in recent weeks, with the number of fixed-rate deals priced below 5% plummeting dramatically. According to data from Moneyfacts, just nine sub-5% fixed-rate mortgages remain available, down from 1,494 at the start of September. This represents a staggering 99% reduction, excluding products exclusive to Northern Ireland. The rapid repricing of mortgage deals has left borrowers facing higher costs, with average rates reaching levels not seen in three years.

Rising Mortgage Rates Hit Borrowers

The average five-year fixed-rate mortgage has now climbed to 6%, its highest level since September 2023, whilst the average two-year fix has risen to 5.98%, reaching a peak last seen in December 2023. These increases come as major lenders, including Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Nationwide, NatWest, Santander, and TSB, implemented multiple rate hikes throughout September. Barclays, for example, raised selected fixed rates four times, whilst others made three rounds of increases.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, commented on the impact of these changes: "The disappearance of around 1,500 sub-5% fixed-rate deals since the start of September has been brutal. Average fixed mortgage rates returning to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers." She added that those approaching the end of their current fixed-term deal should carefully compare their options, as some lenders allow customers to secure a new deal several months in advance.

Impact on Buyers and Homeowners

The sharp rise in mortgage rates is likely to put further pressure on buyer affordability and transaction volumes. Ian Harris, president of NAEA Propertymark, noted that estate agents are already witnessing the effects of higher mortgage costs. "Buyers are highly sensitive to mortgage rates, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals will inevitably add further pressure to affordability," he said. "For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments could mean reducing their budget or stepping back from a purchase altogether."

Variable-rate mortgages have proven more resilient during this period, with the number of deals priced below 5% slipping from 411 to 389 in September. However, including Northern Ireland-only products, the mortgage market lost 1,610 sub-5% fixed and variable options over the month. Rising gilt yields and volatile swap rates have been cited as key factors driving up lenders' wholesale funding costs, leaving them with less scope to offer cheaper fixed-rate deals.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, these developments highlight the importance of staying informed and exploring all available options. With mortgage rates continuing to fluctuate, securing a competitive deal may require careful planning and timely action.

item.title: Rental yields climb towards 8% as portfolios grow
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Buy-to-let rental yields across England and Wales have climbed to 7.9% on average in the third quarter of 2023, according to the latest figures from Fleet Mortgages. This marks a notable increase from 7.5% recorded in the same period last year, suggesting resilience in the rental market despite higher mortgage costs. The data also reveals a continuing trend towards larger property portfolios, with the average landlord now owning 18 buy-to-let properties compared to just 12 twelve months ago.

Regional variations in rental yields

Yorkshire & Humber emerged as the highest-yielding region with average returns of 9.3%, followed closely by the North East at 9.2%. The East Midlands (8.4%), North West (8.3%) and West Midlands (8.2%) also demonstrated strong performance. Only two regions - the North West and Wales - saw annual yields decline slightly.

London continues to offer the lowest yields at 6.4%, though this represents an improvement from 5.9% last year. The capital maintains its position as the most expensive rental market, with average monthly rents reaching £2,597 - almost 10% higher than the previous quarter. item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The Property Ombudsman (TPO) has strengthened its leadership team with the addition of two seasoned property professionals to its board of directors. Jan Hÿtch and Bill Cooper bring a combined 70 years of industry expertise to their new non-executive roles at the consumer redress body.

Vast industry experience

With over three decades in residential property, Jan Hÿtch offers comprehensive knowledge of agency operations and professional standards. Her career includes 30 years as a partner at Arnolds Keys LLP followed by roles with Propertymark and the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors. Hÿtch has served on TPO's Industry Forum since 2018 and currently leads member services at Propertymark.

Bill Cooper complements this with extensive governance experience from his time as an equity partner at Deloitte and KPMG, advising leadership teams on strategic matters. His hands-on property knowledge comes from owning a Martin & Co franchise in Oxford, where he expanded operations through acquisitions before becoming a landlord and property investor.

Strengthening consumer protection

TPO chair Claire Bassett welcomed the appointments, noting both directors' deep understanding of professional standards and consumer redress mechanisms. Their combined expertise comes at a time when property businesses face increasing scrutiny over complaint handling and service quality.

For homeowners and tenants, these appointments signal TPO's commitment to maintaining robust dispute resolution processes. The ombudsman scheme plays a crucial role in resolving complaints about estate agents, lettings professionals and property management firms across England and Wales.

Meanwhile, in separate industry news, Rightmove has announced board changes including the appointment of former Barratt Redrow chief executive David Thomas. Such movements often indicate strategic shifts in how property platforms engage with both industry professionals and consumers.

For borrowers and property seekers, these leadership changes at major industry bodies may influence future standards and service levels across the sector. Homeowners might monitor how these appointments affect complaint resolution timescales and the overall consumer experience when dealing with property professionals.

item.title: Estate agents offered automated For Sale board management through CRM integration
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The process of managing For Sale and To Let boards has become significantly more streamlined for UK estate agents, thanks to a new automated service now integrated with several major customer relationship management (CRM) systems. This innovation could save agents considerable time by eliminating manual board ordering and tracking tasks.

How the automated board service works

A partnership between National Independent Board Services (NIBS) and property technology firm openmoove has enabled automatic board management through popular CRMs including Alto, Street, Rex, Loop and Apex27. The system monitors property status changes within an agent's CRM platform, then triggers appropriate actions for associated signage without requiring manual input.

For instance, when a property's status changes to 'sold' or 'let', the system automatically arranges board removal. This feature aims to reduce the number of forgotten signs left outside properties after transactions complete. Agents also receive photographic confirmation when boards are installed or collected.

Benefits for estate agents

The service offers several advantages for busy agency offices:

  • Eliminates duplicate data entry by syncing with existing CRM systems
  • Provides nationwide coverage through NIBS's network of independent board companies
  • Includes comprehensive reporting and stock management tools
  • Consolidates invoicing across multiple branches

Sue Low of Cannell Signs, an NIBS member company, commented: "Local board companies have always offered superior service with our own print facilities and vehicles. The missing element was national coordination - now agents can manage boards anywhere in the country through one simple CRM update."

The future of property marketing

This development represents part of a broader shift towards automation in property transactions. As Ross McKenzie of openmoove noted: "For Sale boards remain the starting point for most home sales, yet until now, managing them involved unnecessary manual processes. Our integration makes this automatic within agents' existing systems at no additional cost."

Looking ahead, the partners aim to expand the service to more CRM platforms while developing further features to streamline the entire property transaction process. For estate agents, such innovations could mean less administrative work and more time to focus on client relationships.

With over 5,000 agency offices already served by NIBS members including several regional specialists, this automated approach may soon become standard practice across the UK property market.

item.title: Cost of rental voids up 58% in three years
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The financial impact of rental void periods has increased dramatically across the UK private rental sector, with landlords facing significantly longer periods of empty properties and lost income. Recent analysis reveals the average cost of rental voids has surged by 58% over the past three years, creating substantial pressure for property investors.

Understanding the growing void period challenge

Void periods – the time between tenancies when a rental property sits empty – have become notably more expensive for landlords. Several factors contribute to this trend, including:

  • Longer average void durations compared to pre-pandemic levels
  • Higher mortgage interest rates increasing holding costs
  • Rising property maintenance expenses during vacant periods
  • Increased local authority licensing requirements in some areas

Industry experts suggest that void periods which previously lasted weeks may now extend to several months in certain regions, particularly where rental demand has softened or where landlords need to undertake significant property upgrades between tenancies.

Strategies to mitigate void period costs

While void periods are an inevitable part of property investment, landlords might consider several approaches to minimise their financial impact:

  • Market research: Keeping rental prices competitive through regular local market reviews could help attract tenants more quickly
  • Property presentation: Investing in professional photography and staging may make properties more appealing to prospective renters
  • Flexible tenancies: Offering different contract lengths might appeal to a broader range of tenants
  • Pre-emptive maintenance: Addressing repair issues during tenancies could reduce turnaround time between lets

Some landlords are exploring alternative rental models such as corporate lets or short-term holiday rentals (subject to local regulations) to reduce void periods, though these approaches come with their own considerations and potential risks.

As the private rental sector continues to evolve, landlords may need to adapt their strategies to manage the growing financial impact of void periods. Keeping abreast of local market conditions and maintaining properties to a high standard could prove crucial in navigating this challenging environment.

item.title: Inheritance boom could bring thousands more landlords
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A surge in inheritances across the UK could lead to a significant rise in the number of landlords, as intergenerational wealth transfers open doors to property investment opportunities. With younger generations increasingly benefiting from inherited assets, many may consider entering the buy-to-let market to grow their wealth further.

The Impact of Rising Inheritances

Recent trends indicate that wealth transfers from older to younger generations are on the rise. As baby boomers pass on their assets, a growing number of individuals are finding themselves in a position to invest in property. For some, this could mean purchasing additional homes to let, potentially boosting the private rental sector.

Whilst inheritances provide a financial springboard, becoming a landlord requires careful consideration. Prospective investors might weigh up factors such as mortgage options, rental yields, and the responsibilities of managing a property. Additionally, changes in tax regulations and evolving tenant rights could influence decisions in this area.

Opportunities and Challenges in Buy-to-Let

For those considering entering the buy-to-let market, there are both opportunities and challenges to navigate. On one hand, rising property prices in certain regions could offer long-term capital growth, whilst rental demand remains strong in many areas. On the other hand, increased regulation and higher costs, such as stamp duty and maintenance expenses, may pose hurdles for new landlords.

Borrowers might explore specialist buy-to-let mortgages, which are tailored to property investors. These products often require larger deposits and come with different eligibility criteria compared to residential mortgages. Seeking professional financial advice could help individuals make informed decisions about whether buy-to-let is the right path for them.

As the property market continues to evolve, inheritances could play a pivotal role in shaping its future. For those with newfound wealth, investing in property may be an appealing option, but thorough research and planning remain essential to success.

item.title: Holiday let profit lost if reclassification goes ahead – claim
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Proposed tax changes for holiday lets could significantly reduce profitability for property investors and impact local economies in tourism-reliant areas, according to recent analysis. The potential reclassification of short-term rental properties may alter the financial landscape for those operating in this sector.

Potential impact on holiday let returns

Industry experts suggest that the planned tax adjustments might substantially decrease net yields for holiday let owners. Current projections indicate that some operators could see their profits diminish by nearly a quarter if the reforms proceed as outlined. The changes primarily concern how properties are categorised for tax purposes, potentially shifting many holiday lets into a higher taxation bracket.

These adjustments come as the government examines ways to balance the holiday let market with the need for residential housing in popular tourist destinations. However, critics argue the measures may inadvertently harm smaller operators whilst failing to address underlying housing shortages.

Concerns for tourism-dependent communities

Local economies in coastal towns and rural hotspots may face particular challenges if the tax changes discourage holiday let investments. Many businesses in these areas – from cafes to activity providers – rely heavily on visitors staying in short-term rentals. A reduction in available holiday accommodation could lead to fewer tourists and lower spending in these regions.

Industry bodies have highlighted that the proposed reforms might disproportionately affect certain areas. Cornwall, the Lake District and other popular staycation destinations could see significant economic repercussions if property owners reconsider their investment strategies due to reduced profitability.

Considering alternative property strategies

Property investors concerned about the potential changes might explore diversifying their portfolios. Some options could include shifting focus to traditional buy-to-let properties, exploring commercial hospitality investments, or considering properties in areas less likely to be affected by tourism taxes.

Those currently operating holiday lets may wish to review their financial projections and consult professional advisers to understand how the proposed changes could affect their specific circumstances. Many experts recommend staying informed about the consultation process, as the final details of any reforms may differ from initial proposals.

While the government's intention appears to be creating a fairer property market, the balance between regulating the sector and supporting local tourism economies remains a complex challenge. The consultation period may provide opportunities for stakeholders to share their perspectives before any final decisions are made.

item.title: September house price growth halves
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK housing market has shown signs of slowing down, with Nationwide’s latest report revealing that house price growth halved in September. Rising mortgage costs appear to be a key factor influencing buyer demand and market activity, creating a more subdued environment for property values.

Understanding the slowdown

According to Nationwide’s data, the pace of house price growth has significantly decreased, with September’s figures showing a marked reduction compared to previous months. This slowdown suggests that affordability pressures, particularly driven by higher mortgage rates, are beginning to weigh on potential buyers. Many homeowners and prospective purchasers might be reconsidering their plans amidst these financial challenges.

Additionally, the broader economic climate, including inflation and rising living costs, could be contributing to this trend. With household budgets under strain, the ability to save for deposits or afford higher monthly mortgage payments has become more difficult for some buyers.

The impact of rising mortgage costs

Mortgage rates have been climbing steadily, influenced by the Bank of England’s base rate increases. This has led to higher borrowing costs for those looking to secure new mortgages or remortgage existing ones. For first-time buyers, in particular, these rising costs could be a significant barrier to entering the property market.

Existing homeowners may also face challenges if they are nearing the end of fixed-rate mortgage deals. With remortgaging potentially leading to higher monthly payments, some borrowers might find themselves needing to reassess their financial plans. Seeking independent financial advice could be a prudent step for those navigating these changes.

What does this mean for the housing market?

While the slowdown in house price growth may offer some relief to buyers who have been struggling with affordability, it also highlights the complexities of the current market. Sellers might need to adjust their expectations, recognising that the rapid price increases seen in recent years may not be sustainable in the current climate.

For those considering entering the market, it could be worth exploring fixed-rate mortgage options to lock in current rates and provide stability against potential future increases. Additionally, staying informed about market trends and seeking professional guidance may help borrowers make more informed decisions.

As the UK housing market continues to evolve, keeping a close eye on economic developments and mortgage rate changes will be crucial for both buyers and sellers. While the current slowdown presents challenges, it also offers opportunities for those who are prepared to navigate this shifting landscape.

item.title: Jobs at risk as property giant announces major shake-up
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property consultancy giant JLL has announced plans to close its UK planning division, potentially affecting at least 25 employees across five offices. The restructuring could lead to redundancies in London, Bristol, Manchester, Leeds and Edinburgh as the firm reassesses its business priorities.

Restructuring follows leadership changes

The proposed closure comes after several senior management shifts at JLL. In April 2025, Matt Richards took over as UK chief executive, replacing Stephanie Hyde. This followed his previous role leading capital markets across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. The planning division currently operates under Raoul Veevers, who joined from Cluttons in 2022, and regional lead Joanna Gabrilatsou, a JLL veteran since 2011.

This isn't the first round of job cuts at the consultancy. Just one month after Richards' appointment, JLL eliminated nearly 150 positions within its UK property and asset management operations. The company hasn't disclosed the final number of redundancies expected from this latest restructuring.

Strategic review prompts difficult decisions

In an official statement, JLL explained: "We continually evaluate our business to align services with strategic priorities and client requirements. This has led to the challenging but necessary proposal that some roles may become redundant." The firm emphasised its confidence in existing leadership teams to maintain client service standards during the transition.

The planning division closure forms part of a broader operational review as JLL adapts to changing market conditions. Property professionals affected by the restructuring may wish to explore their options in a sector where demand for planning expertise remains steady, particularly for large-scale development projects.

Homeowners following this development might note that such corporate restructurings can sometimes signal shifting priorities in the property sector. While JLL maintains its commitment to client service, the changes reflect the ongoing evolution of consultancy services in response to economic pressures and changing client demands.

item.title: Landlord loses HMO licence after ignoring letting agent’s fire safety warnings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A Glasgow landlord has been stripped of their House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) licence after failing to address critical fire safety issues, despite warnings from their letting agent. Glasgow City Council’s licensing committee refused to renew Anna McMullan’s licence for a property on Sauchiehall Street following inspections that revealed multiple safety breaches.

Serious Safety Concerns Identified

The property, which housed five tenants, was inspected by both the council’s HMO team and the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service earlier this year. The inspections uncovered numerous hazards, including fire doors that did not close properly, blocked escape routes, and excessive combustible materials stored in utility and shower rooms. Inspectors also noted the absence of fire safety information for tenants, an incomplete electrical installation condition report, and structural issues such as holes in walls and ceilings.

The letting agent informed the committee that they had provided the landlord with several quotes for remedial work, but these were rejected. Despite repeated warnings, the landlord allegedly failed to make the necessary repairs, leaving tenants in a potentially dangerous environment.

Unresolved Issues Lead to Licence Refusal

A follow-up inspection in September revealed that many of the identified issues remained unresolved. Dust and grease had built up on extraction fans, fire doors still did not close correctly, and excessive gaps were found beneath doors. Although contractors had visited the property to quote for repairs, the work had not been completed.

Committee chairman Alex Wilson expressed concern over the lettings agent’s decision to allow new tenants to move into the property in August, despite the outstanding safety concerns. “You’ve put tenants into a property that’s not safe,” he stated, adding that the February inspection had highlighted “a huge number of deficiencies” which should have been rectified.

Lessons for Landlords and Agents

This case underscores the importance of addressing fire safety issues promptly and thoroughly. item.title: Prime London house prices rise for first time in four years as rents accelerate
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Prime central London property prices have shown their first quarterly rise since 2020, according to fresh market data, though economic headwinds continue to cloud the recovery. Knight Frank's latest analysis reveals a 0.3% price increase between July and September, marking a tentative turnaround after four years of declines.

Market Shows Fragile Recovery Signs

The capital's prime property sector appears to be stabilising after facing multiple challenges, including mortgage rate fluctuations, tax reforms and political uncertainty. Whilst annual values remain 2% lower than September 2022, this represents the mildest year-on-year decline witnessed in the past eighteen months. Prime outer London locations have demonstrated greater resilience, with prices dipping just 0.6% over the last twelve months.

Transaction volumes provide further evidence of gradual improvement. The annual decrease in property exchanges across prime London neighbourhoods has slowed to 2.5% - a significant improvement from the 14% annual decline recorded six months earlier. The super-prime market (properties over £10 million) has also stabilised, with transaction numbers holding steady at 121 annually whilst total spending increased by 14% to £2.4 billion.

Shifting Attitudes Among Buyers and Sellers

Market participants appear to be adapting to the new financial landscape. Liza-Jane Kelly of Knight Frank observes that after years of price adjustments, sellers are demonstrating more realistic expectations: "Some properties have been listed for several years, and owners are now prioritising moving forward over holding out for peak prices."

Purchasers, meanwhile, are recognising potential value after significant price corrections. Average values in prime central London remain 22% below their 2015 highs, creating opportunities for buyers who had previously chosen to rent. Kelly notes: "When negative headlines subside, we see how quickly underlying demand resurfaces in this market."

Challenges Remain for London's Prime Market

The abolition of non-dom status earlier this year continues to impact the highest-value segments, whilst the approaching Autumn Budget introduces fresh uncertainty regarding potential property tax changes. These factors, combined with broader economic concerns, suggest the recovery may prove gradual rather than rapid.

For those considering prime London property, the current climate highlights the importance of thorough research and professional advice. Mortgage borrowers might find value in comparing products tailored for high-value purchases, whilst both buyers and sellers may wish to stay informed about potential tax developments that could affect their financial planning.

item.title: Preparing your rental property for winter weather
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As temperatures begin to drop across the UK, landlords may wish to turn their attention to winter-proofing their rental properties. With the government investing £1.4 billion in flood defences across England for 2026/27, and meteorologists predicting potential extreme weather patterns later this year, preventative maintenance could prove particularly valuable this winter season.

Assessing flood risks and emergency planning

Property owners might consider checking whether their rental falls within a flood risk area. The government's online flood risk service allows searches by postcode, providing valuable insight into potential hazards. For properties in higher-risk locations, compiling an information pack for tenants could be beneficial, including:

  • Local emergency contact numbers
  • Details of community flood action groups
  • Instructions for reporting flooding incidents
  • Links to the government's Personal Flood Plan

Local authority websites often contain specific flood preparedness information, including locations of community hubs and details of flood wardens. Sharing these resources with tenants may help ensure they're prepared should adverse weather strike.

Conducting thorough property inspections

Before winter sets in, landlords might schedule a detailed inspection of their rental property, providing tenants with the required 24-hour notice. Key areas to examine include:

  • Gutters and drainage: Clearing blocked gutters and downpipes can prevent water damage during heavy rainfall
  • Roof condition: Checking for slipped tiles or damaged flashing could prevent leaks during storms
  • Structural integrity: Cracks in pointing or external walls may warrant attention before winter weather exacerbates damage
  • External hazards: Loose fittings, unstable fences or overhanging branches might become dangerous in high winds

Heating systems also deserve particular attention during winter inspections. Landlords may wish to verify that systems are functioning correctly, that tenants understand how to operate them efficiently, and that exposed pipes have adequate insulation. Confirming the location of the stopcock and ensuring empty properties have appropriate frost protection measures could prevent costly winter emergencies.

Whilst the UK's weather remains unpredictable, taking proactive steps to prepare rental properties for winter conditions might help landlords avoid costly repairs and ensure tenant safety throughout the colder months. Regular maintenance not only protects the property investment but also contributes to positive landlord-tenant relationships during potentially challenging weather conditions.

item.title: Estate agency expands lettings portfolio with acquisition of rival firm
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Kent-based Guildcrest Estates has expanded its lettings portfolio through the acquisition of fellow independent agency Frederick & Co Property Services. The strategic move adds roughly 150 managed properties to Guildcrest's books while extending its operational footprint across the Thanet area of Kent.

Strategic expansion in the Kent lettings market

The acquisition aligns with Guildcrest Estates' broader growth strategy, complementing its existing services in residential sales, new homes and commercial property sectors. As part of the transition, one of Frederick & Co's team members will join Guildcrest to maintain continuity for existing landlords and tenants.

Sarah Huskstep, managing director of Guildcrest Estates, emphasised the strategic fit: "This acquisition perfectly complements our current operations. Martyn has developed an impressive property management business with strong client relationships that we're committed to preserving."

Client continuity remains key focus

Frederick & Co's former owner Martyn Stampe highlighted the importance of finding the right cultural match for his business: "Guildcrest shares our dedication to personal service while providing clients with enhanced resources from a growing agency." Stampe expressed pride in the relationships his firm had cultivated with local landlords and tenants over the years.

The enlarged portfolio will be managed by Guildcrest's existing lettings team, supported by the agency's established property management systems. While financial details remain undisclosed, the deal strengthens Guildcrest Group's position as a comprehensive property services provider across East Kent.

For landlords and tenants in the region, the merger may bring access to broader resources while maintaining the personal service associated with independent agencies. Such consolidation in the lettings market could become more common as agencies seek to enhance their service offerings and geographical coverage.

item.title: New estate agency launches for ‘standout’ homes
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The London property market has welcomed a new estate agency with a unique focus on distinctive and design-led homes. Orato Estates aims to cater to vendors whose properties stand out from the crowd, offering something beyond the standard listing. Specialising in restored period properties, architecturally unusual houses, and bespoke apartments, the agency is carving out a niche in a competitive market.

A Focus on Quality Over Quantity

Unlike traditional estate agencies that often prioritise high-volume listings, Orato Estates is taking a more selective approach. The agency plans to curate a smaller portfolio of homes that showcase exceptional architecture, interiors, and individual character. This strategy reflects its philosophy that "some homes are special because someone has put love into them." Andreas Abasaid, the agency’s founder, brings a wealth of experience from luxury marketing, creative industries, and entrepreneurship, shaping Orato’s unique vision.

Abasaid explains, “We wanted to create an agency for homes that don’t neatly fit into the traditional property box. These are properties where every detail has been thoughtfully considered, leaving a lasting impression on anyone who walks through the door.” This approach emphasises editorial-style marketing, focusing on storytelling and design rather than competing on listing numbers alone.

Building Relationships in the Property Market

Initially focusing on London, Orato Estates plans to collaborate with private sellers, developers, and industry professionals. The agency aims to build strong relationships with architects and interior designers, sourcing properties that align with its ethos. By partnering with creatives, Orato hopes to uncover homes with a unique narrative and aesthetic appeal.

The launch of Orato Estates highlights a growing trend in London’s property market, where agencies are increasingly differentiating themselves through specialised niches. For homeowners with standout properties, this could be an opportunity to work with an agency that truly understands and values their home’s individuality.

As the property landscape evolves, agencies like Orato Estates are redefining how exceptional homes are marketed and sold. For those with distinctive properties, it could be worth exploring this new approach to property presentation.
